title: We Won't Get the Same Future Update
summary: As personal agents accumulate failures and choices as memories, rules, and code, they branch into distinct lineages. The core role of platforms shifts toward managing the ownership and merging of those lineages.
content:
I open Telegram and ask my agent to build things. It has been a long time since I stopped looking at the code anyway, and I still haven't found a more efficient setup for simple, responsive development, whether at the office or anywhere away from home. 

All I have to do is repeat a loop: tell it what I want to build, what bothers me about the current result, and what needs to be checked before we can call it done. Unless I'm in public, I hardly type at all. I press the microphone button and pour out my thoughts in my own voice. “No… undo that last thing and go this way.” Even the traces of changing my mind, as if talking to myself. Speaking is more than three times faster than typing, but there is another advantage: the agent follows my train of thought better when I let it hear my thoughts before they are organized, rather than give it neatly composed sentences.

I develop with Hermes Agent. Because recurring tasks automatically turn into skills, something that took several sentences to explain last month takes just one today. This structural advantage is probably what pushed it past OpenClaw into first place in agent usage.

The biggest difference between today's agentic development and the way I worked until late last year, launching Claude Code or Codex directly in a terminal, is not the model's intelligence. It is that memories of my work, development habits, tools and instructions for using them, completion criteria, and recovery methods are already connected on top of the model. Within a single run, this layer coordinates which models and tools to call, which specialist agents to hand work to, what context to pass along, and where to stop and ask me for confirmation. This is the control over execution that the industry calls orchestration.

If the model is the brain, this layer decides which memories it wakes up with today, what to watch out for, and where to stop. A better model can be swapped in whenever one comes out. The ways of working we develop together, on the other hand, are not so easily replaced. The center of gravity of personalization lies not in the model, but in what accumulates outside it.

So the thing I say most often to my agent is not a request for a new feature.

“Fix the structure so you don't make that same mistake next time.”

Then the agent does more than correct a single wrong answer. It looks back to see whether it lacked memory, whether a rule was ambiguous, or whether the completion criteria were too loose. It revises its memory and skills and adds regression tests. At some point, my agent began rewriting its own operating rules and recovery logic, sometimes even the core code of Hermes itself.

When I switched from OpenClaw to Hermes this spring, there was no way to connect my five agents, which I call Jeon, Sion, Mion, Sano, and Raon, to their own Telegram bots. So I changed the code myself to let one gateway handle multiple profiles and load a different personality, memory, and session for each bot. If the wrong account came in, I blocked the response entirely rather than pass it to another bot. Once memories get mixed up, the premise of personalization falls apart. The official Hermes implementation was made public on June 18 and included in the next day's release. Now, turning on an option in the official version lets one gateway manage bots across multiple profiles. We ended up in the same place, but in the meantime, my own code filled the gap.

I also changed the tool that calls several frontier models at once. I put a timeout on each call so one slow model would not stall everything, and kept the answers that arrived first rather than discard them. To address the problem of assuming a task was done when work remained, I added a safeguard that prevents it from declaring completion while any items are unfinished. When a long task gets interrupted, I made it always leave behind its reasoning and intermediate results. Each time we encountered the same failure, it was not just the memory that grew. The code for handling the next failure changed.

After countless revisions like these, the Hermes I use has moved quite far from stock Hermes. It started from the same seed, but grew into a different branch, fed by my nagging and trial and error. MemKraft, the agent memory system I built myself, also stores more than what was decided. It keeps the reasons behind a judgment, the outcome, and how long that information can be trusted. What I review is closer to the reasons for a change than the code itself.

As this continues, the meaning of software personalization will change considerably. Until now, personalization meant choosing things like icon arrangements, background colors, and keyboard shortcuts within a finished piece of software. When you live and work with an agent, experience does not remain only as memory. That memory changes rules, creates tests for validation and new tools, and rewrites recovery logic and the codebase itself. Settings preserve preferences. Code preserves the way a person has failed and recovered.

That is why orchestration alone is not enough to describe this. Orchestration adjusts the sequence and branches within a given run. What I am seeing is a stage where the memories, rules, and code surrounding that run move on to their next version through experience. 

I would like to call this branching into individual histories Agent Lineage. An agent that starts from the same foundation translates one person's choices and failures into a form that can be verified and reversed, branching into a lineage of its own.

This also breaks the assumption that everyone uses the same kind of agent. An update is no longer a matter of overwriting everything with a finished new version. It becomes a matter of merging the shared features the platform has fixed with the changes I have cultivated. Even if everyone gets the same Hermes 2.0, one person's agent checks three times before making a payment, another breaks work into smaller pieces, and another asks a question first when a request is vague. It is not just the screen that differs. Some of the underlying ways they work are different.

The role of agent platforms changes entirely, too. Instead of distributing finished products, they become places where lineages grow. They need to accept security updates to the shared foundation while preserving the rules that have changed to resemble me, merge personal code with the official version when they conflict, and selectively undo changes learned incorrectly while keeping the memories. Their competitive strength will come less from the number of features than from the ability to safely manage inheritance, merging, validation, and rollback across millions of branching lineages.

This structure, which I first experienced in development, will spread into daily life. Schedules and relationships, travel and purchases, health and work are now scattered across different apps. A personal agent follows us between them, stitching together the context of one person's life. The route I disliked on my last trip and my habit of not making plans the day after a long meeting meet in the same memory. As memories accumulate, behavior changes. As behavior repeats, rules and code emerge that fit only that person.

Even two people who receive the same agent will get entirely different answers to the same request a few months later. “Pick a place to stay this weekend that I'd like.” One person's agent books a small hotel in the old part of town with no view. That is because what stayed with him from his travels was a bakery in an alley at dawn and an old bookstore. The other person's agent chooses a secluded place by the sea without a single restaurant nearby. It remembers that her favorite part of the last trip was the afternoon she canceled all her plans and listened only to the waves. Once different records of a life sit behind the same sentence, the right answers diverge, too.

Paradoxically, the more software branches from person to person, the more important the shared foundation becomes. To move between services and actually take action, identity and permissions, payments and records, auditing and undoing must share the same grammar. Personal code may differ, but the interfaces where they meet must be solid. Rather than disappear, today's SaaS will likely recede behind the screen and become the foundation of official records and accountability that agents rely on.

At that point, the most important question will not be which model you use. Who owns the rules and code that have changed alongside me, the lineage formed through failures? Can I take all of it with me when I move to another platform? A good platform will not be one that sells the single smartest agent. It will be one that ensures the lineage that has grown differently for each person belongs to that person to the very end.

I press the microphone button. “No, undo that.” One hesitation, casually added, becomes a memory, becomes a rule, and changes a line of code in the agent's bones.
